intro: Why does a new sneaker sell out in a minute and then show up online for double the price? Why does gas cost more in summer? Why does a store with rivals down the street keep cutting prices? Each of these is a market in action. Buyers and sellers meet, and a price comes out of their choices.

In this unit you will read small tables of prices and quantities. You will find the price where buyers and sellers agree. You will tell a shift of a curve from a slide along it. Then you will step inside a business. You will add up revenue, subtract costs and find the profit, using a school store as the example.

By the end, you will be able to explain a real price change in three steps. You will also be able to say why more sellers usually help buyers, what a monopoly is, and why governments watch for businesses that block competition.
bigQuestion: How do buyers, sellers and competition work together to set prices and decide what gets made?

timeline.t: Adam Smith publishes The Wealth of Nations, explaining how markets and self-interest work
David Ricardo publishes his Principles of Political Economy and Taxation
The Chicago Board of Trade opens, a market for grain from Midwest farms
Alfred Marshall's Principles of Economics uses supply and demand curves
Congress passes the Sherman Antitrust Act to protect competition
The Federal Reserve Act creates the Federal Reserve, with a Reserve Bank in Chicago
The Clayton Antitrust Act adds more rules against blocking competition
The National Labor Relations Act protects most private workers' right to form unions
The Fair Labor Standards Act sets the first federal minimum wage
The federal minimum wage rises to $7.25 an hour

test.q: The price of a video game drops from $60 to $40, and more people buy it. What is this?
test.why: Only the game's own price changed, so buyers slid along the demand curve.

test.q: Example market: at $6, buyers want 70 and sellers offer 70. What is $6?
test.why: Equilibrium is where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.

test.q: Example: at $9, buyers want 30 and sellers offer 75. What is the result?
test.why: 75 minus 30 equals a surplus of 45 units.

test.q: The cost of flour rises sharply. What happens to the supply of bread?
test.why: Flour is an input cost. Higher input costs shift supply left.

test.q: A popular singer posts a video wearing a brand of hat. What happens to demand for that hat?
test.why: A change in tastes raises demand at every price, a shift right.

test.q: Tickets to a big game sell out instantly at $40 (example price). What does this suggest?
test.why: A sellout is a shortage, which happens when the price is below equilibrium.

test.q: A juice stand sells 60 cups at $2 and has $70 in costs (example numbers). What is its profit?
test.why: Revenue is 60 times $2, or $120. Profit is $120 minus $70, or $50.

test.q: What does the supply curve look like on a graph?
choices: It slopes down from left to right
It slopes up from left to right
test.why: Sellers offer more at higher prices, so the supply curve rises from left to right.

test.q: Which business type is owned by shareholders?
test.why: Shareholders own shares of stock in a corporation.

test.q: Why do more sellers usually mean lower prices?
choices: Sellers compete for the same buyers
test.why: Competition gives each seller a reason to cut prices or improve to win buyers.

test.q: Two rival stores secretly agree to charge the same high price. Which law does this break?
test.why: Price-fixing among rivals is banned by antitrust laws.

test.q: A worker earns $18 an hour for 15 hours (example wage). What does she earn before taxes?
The price of hamburgers, a substitute for hot dogs, rises. What happens to demand for hot dogs?
choices: Supply of hot dogs shifts left
test.why: When a substitute costs more, buyers switch to the other good, so its demand rises.

test.q: A store raises a snack price from $1 to $2 and sales fall from 100 to 40 (example). What happens to revenue?
test.why: Revenue was $1 times 100, or $100. Now it is $2 times 40, or $80.

test.q: What does an entrepreneur get if a risky new business succeeds?
test.why: Profit is the reward for taking the risk of starting a business.

write.prompt: Your school store sells 200 water bottles a week at $1 each (example numbers), and each costs $0.40. A second store opens nearby. Should your store cut its price to $0.80, keep it at $1, or add something new? Use numbers for revenue and profit, and name the trade-offs.
tips: Find revenue (price times quantity) and profit (revenue minus costs) for each choice.
Say how the law of demand affects how many bottles you sell at each price.
Explain what competition from the second store changes.
Name the opportunity cost of the choice you make.
End with a clear decision and one reason it could go wrong.
